items.readable_text:
Content:
We can apply the logical operations of conjunction and disjunction to predicates.

Content:
- The conjunction of the predicates [MATH: P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)] and [MATH: Q(y_1,y_2,\ldots,y_m)] is a new predicate which we denote as follows:
[MATH: P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n) \land Q(y_1,y_2,\ldots,y_m)]
This conjunction is true whenever [MATH: P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)] is true and [MATH: Q(y_1,y_2,\ldots,y_m)] is true for a specific set of respective variable assignments. The conjunction is false if either [MATH: P] or [MATH: Q] is false.
- The disjunction of the predicates [MATH: P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)] and [MATH: Q(y_1,y_2,\ldots,y_m)] is written as follows:
[MATH: P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n) \lor Q(y_1,y_2,\ldots,y_m)]
This disjunction is true whenever [MATH: P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)] is true, [MATH: Q(y_1,y_2,\ldots,y_m)] is true, or both are true, for a specific set of variable assignments. The disjunction is false if [MATH: P] and [MATH: Q] are false.

Content:
For example, consider the following predicates:

Content:
- [MATH: P(n):] [MATH: n] is even
- [MATH: Q(n):] [MATH: n] is positive

Content:
Then, [MATH: P(n) \land Q(n)] is a new predicate that reads "[MATH: n] is even and [MATH: n] is positive," which can be simplified to "[MATH: n] is even and positive."

Content:
On the other hand, [MATH: P(n) \lor Q(n)] is a new predicate that reads "[MATH: n] is even or [MATH: n] is positive," which can be simplified to "[MATH: n] is even or positive."

Content:
When it's clear that [MATH: P(n)] is a predicate in the variable [MATH: n,] we sometimes omit the variables when writing them. So, [MATH: P(n) \land Q(n)] and [MATH: P(n) \lor Q(n)] can be written as [MATH: P \land Q] and [MATH: P \lor Q,] respectively.

items.title: Expressing a Compound Predicate in Symbolic Form

sections.normalized_html:
Consider the following compound predicates:

[MATH: x] is even and divisible by [MATH: 5.]

[MATH: x] is even or less than [MATH: 6].

Express these compound predicates above in symbolic form given the following notations:

  • [MATH: A(x):] [MATH: x] is even

  • [MATH: B(x):] [MATH: x] is divisible by [MATH: 5]

  • [MATH: C(x):] [MATH: x] is less than [MATH: 6]

items.title: Expressing a Nested Compound Predicate in Symbolic Form

sections.normalized_html:
Consider the following compound predicate:

[MATH: x] is positive and a multiple of [MATH: 4,] or [MATH: x] is negative.

Express this compound predicate in symbolic form given the following notations:

  • [MATH: P(x):] [MATH: x] is positive

  • [MATH: M(x):] [MATH: x] is a multiple of [MATH: 4]

  • [MATH: N(x):] [MATH: x] is negative
sections.readable_text:
Consider the following compound predicate:

> [MATH: x] is positive and a multiple of [MATH: 4,] or [MATH: x] is negative.

Express this compound predicate in symbolic form given the following notations:

- [MATH: P(x):] [MATH: x] is positive
- [MATH: M(x):] [MATH: x] is a multiple of [MATH: 4]
- [MATH: N(x):] [MATH: x] is negative

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The word "and" is represented by the symbol "[MATH: \land,]" while the word "or" is represented by the symbol "[MATH: \lor.]"

Note that this sentence consists of two parts:

  • Part 1: [MATH: x] is positive and a multiple of [MATH: 4.] This corresponds to [MATH: \underbrace{x \,\textrm{is positive}}_P \quad \underbrace{\vphantom{p}\textrm{and}}_{\land} \quad \underbrace{x \vphantom{p}\textrm{ is a multiple of }4 }_M,] that is, [MATH: P \land M.]

  • Part 2: [MATH: x] is negative. This corresponds to [MATH: N.]

So, we can express the sentence as [MATH: \underbrace{x \,\textrm{ is positive}\,\textrm{and a multiple of }4 }_{P \land M} \quad \underbrace{\vphantom{p}\textrm{or}}_{\lor} \quad \underbrace{x \vphantom{p}\textrm{ is negative} }_N,] that is, [MATH: (P \land M) \lor N.]

Content:
Let [MATH: T_P] and [MATH: T_Q] be the truth sets of the predicates [MATH: P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)] and [MATH: Q(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n),] respectively. Note that we're assuming our predicates have the same universal set.

Content:
From the definition of the conjunction of predicates, we have that [MATH: P \land Q] is true if both [MATH: P] and [MATH: Q] are true. Therefore, the truth set of [MATH: P \land Q] is the intersection of the truth sets of [MATH: P] and [MATH: Q{:}]

Content:
[MATH: T_{P \land Q} = T_P \cap T_Q]

Content:
For example, consider the following predicates defined over the set of positive integers:

Content:
- [MATH: P(x):] [MATH: x] is divisible by [MATH: 3]
- [MATH: Q(x):] [MATH: 24] is divisible by [MATH: x]

Content:
We start by finding the truth sets of [MATH: P(x)] and [MATH: Q(x){:}]

Content:

[MATH: T_P = \big\{ 3,6,9,12,15,18,21,24,27 \ldots \big\}.]
- The truth set of [MATH: Q(x)] is
[MATH: T_Q = \big\{ 1,2,3,4,6,8,12,24 \big\}.]

Content:
Therefore, we have

[MATH: T_{P∧Q}|= T_{P}∩T_{Q}; = {3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18, 21, 24, 27…}∩{1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 24}; = {3, 6, 12, 24}.]

Conjunction and disjunction of predicates are generalizations of logical operations on statements. Moreover, the properties of these operations on statements can be translated to corresponding operations on predicates.

Content:
In particular, the idempotent, absorption, associative, and commutative laws also apply to conjunction and disjunction of predicates.

Content:
So, for predicates [MATH: P(x_1,x_2\ldots,x_n),] [MATH: Q(y_1,y_2\ldots,y_m),] and [MATH: R(z_1,z_2\ldots,z_p),] we have the following:

[MATH: P∧P≡P∨P≡P]
- The Associative Laws:
[MATH: P∧(Q∧R)|≡(P∧Q)∧R; P∨(Q∨R)|≡(P∨Q)∨R]
- The Commutative Laws:
[MATH: P∧Q|≡Q∧P; P∨Q|≡Q∨P]
- The Distributive Laws:
[MATH: P∧(Q∨R)|≡(P∧Q)∨(P∧R); P∨(Q∧R)|≡(P∨Q)∧(P∨R)]
- The Absorption Laws:
[MATH: P∧(P∨Q)|≡P; P∨(P∧Q)|≡P]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
We can apply the logical operations of conjunction and disjunction to predicates.

Content:
- The conjunction of the predicates [MATH: P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)] and [MATH: Q(y_1,y_2,\ldots,y_m)] is a new predicate which we denote as follows:
[MATH: P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n) \land Q(y_1,y_2,\ldots,y_m)]
This conjunction is true whenever [MATH: P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)] is true and [MATH: Q(y_1,y_2,\ldots,y_m)] is true for a specific set of respective variable assignments. The conjunction is false if either [MATH: P] or [MATH: Q] is false.
- The disjunction of the predicates [MATH: P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)] and [MATH: Q(y_1,y_2,\ldots,y_m)] is written as follows:
[MATH: P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n) \lor Q(y_1,y_2,\ldots,y_m)]
This disjunction is true whenever [MATH: P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)] is true, [MATH: Q(y_1,y_2,\ldots,y_m)] is true, or both are true, for a specific set of variable assignments. The disjunction is false if [MATH: P] and [MATH: Q] are false.

Content:
For example, consider the following predicates:

Content:
- [MATH: P(n):] [MATH: n] is even
- [MATH: Q(n):] [MATH: n] is positive

Content:
Then, [MATH: P(n) \land Q(n)] is a new predicate that reads "[MATH: n] is even and [MATH: n] is positive," which can be simplified to "[MATH: n] is even and positive."

Content:
On the other hand, [MATH: P(n) \lor Q(n)] is a new predicate that reads "[MATH: n] is even or [MATH: n] is positive," which can be simplified to "[MATH: n] is even or positive."

Content:
When it's clear that [MATH: P(n)] is a predicate in the variable [MATH: n,] we sometimes omit the variables when writing them. So, [MATH: P(n) \land Q(n)] and [MATH: P(n) \lor Q(n)] can be written as [MATH: P \land Q] and [MATH: P \lor Q,] respectively.

---

Item 2 — Example: Expressing a Compound Predicate in Symbolic Form

Example Prompt:
Consider the following compound predicates:

> [MATH: x] is even and divisible by [MATH: 5.]
>
> [MATH: x] is even or less than [MATH: 6].

Express these compound predicates above in symbolic form given the following notations:

- [MATH: A(x):] [MATH: x] is even
- [MATH: B(x):] [MATH: x] is divisible by [MATH: 5]
- [MATH: C(x):] [MATH: x] is less than [MATH: 6]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The word "and" is represented by the symbol "[MATH: \land.]"

So, the first sentence reads

[MATH: 5]

that is, [MATH: A \land B.]

Moreover, the word "or" is represented by the symbol "[MATH: \lor.]"

So, the second sentence reads

[MATH: 6]

that is, [MATH: A \lor C.]

---

Item 5 — Example: Expressing a Nested Compound Predicate in Symbolic Form

Example Prompt:
Consider the following compound predicate:

> [MATH: x] is positive and a multiple of [MATH: 4,] or [MATH: x] is negative.

Express this compound predicate in symbolic form given the following notations:

- [MATH: P(x):] [MATH: x] is positive
- [MATH: M(x):] [MATH: x] is a multiple of [MATH: 4]
- [MATH: N(x):] [MATH: x] is negative

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The word "and" is represented by the symbol "[MATH: \land,]" while the word "or" is represented by the symbol "[MATH: \lor.]"

Note that this sentence consists of two parts:

- Part 1: [MATH: x] is positive and a multiple of [MATH: 4.] This corresponds to
[MATH: \underbrace{x \,\textrm{is positive}}_P \quad \underbrace{\vphantom{p}\textrm{and}}_{\land} \quad \underbrace{x \vphantom{p}\textrm{ is a multiple of }4 }_M,]
that is, [MATH: P \land M.]
- Part 2: [MATH: x] is negative. This corresponds to [MATH: N.]

So, we can express the sentence as
[MATH: \underbrace{x \,\textrm{ is positive}\,\textrm{and a multiple of }4 }_{P \land M} \quad \underbrace{\vphantom{p}\textrm{or}}_{\lor} \quad \underbrace{x \vphantom{p}\textrm{ is negative} }_N,]
that is, [MATH: (P \land M) \lor N.]

Item 8 — Tutorial: The Truth Set of a Conjunction

Content:
Let [MATH: T_P] and [MATH: T_Q] be the truth sets of the predicates [MATH: P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)] and [MATH: Q(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n),] respectively. Note that we're assuming our predicates have the same universal set.

Content:
From the definition of the conjunction of predicates, we have that [MATH: P \land Q] is true if both [MATH: P] and [MATH: Q] are true. Therefore, the truth set of [MATH: P \land Q] is the intersection of the truth sets of [MATH: P] and [MATH: Q{:}]

Content:
[MATH: T_{P \land Q} = T_P \cap T_Q]

Content:
For example, consider the following predicates defined over the set of positive integers:

Content:
- [MATH: P(x):] [MATH: x] is divisible by [MATH: 3]
- [MATH: Q(x):] [MATH: 24] is divisible by [MATH: x]

Content:
We start by finding the truth sets of [MATH: P(x)] and [MATH: Q(x){:}]

Content:
- The truth set of [MATH: P(x)] is
[MATH: T_P = \big\{ 3,6,9,12,15,18,21,24,27 \ldots \big\}.]
- The truth set of [MATH: Q(x)] is
[MATH: T_Q = \big\{ 1,2,3,4,6,8,12,24 \big\}.]

Content:
Therefore, we have

Content:
[MATH: T_{P∧Q}|= T_{P}∩T_{Q}; = {3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18, 21, 24, 27…}∩{1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 24}; = {3, 6, 12, 24}.]

---

Item 9 — Tutorial: The Truth Set of a Disjunction

Content:
Once again, let [MATH: T_P] and [MATH: T_Q] be the truth sets of the predicates [MATH: P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)] and [MATH: Q(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n),] respectively.

Item 13 — Tutorial: Laws Involving Conjunction and Disjunction of Predicates

Content:
Conjunction and disjunction of predicates are generalizations of logical operations on statements. Moreover, the properties of these operations on statements can be translated to corresponding operations on predicates.

Content:
In particular, the idempotent, absorption, associative, and commutative laws also apply to conjunction and disjunction of predicates.

Content:
So, for predicates [MATH: P(x_1,x_2\ldots,x_n),] [MATH: Q(y_1,y_2\ldots,y_m),] and [MATH: R(z_1,z_2\ldots,z_p),] we have the following:

Content:
- The Idempotent Laws:
[MATH: P∧P≡P∨P≡P]
- The Associative Laws:
[MATH: P∧(Q∧R)|≡(P∧Q)∧R; P∨(Q∨R)|≡(P∨Q)∨R]
- The Commutative Laws:
[MATH: P∧Q|≡Q∧P; P∨Q|≡Q∨P]
- The Distributive Laws:
[MATH: P∧(Q∨R)|≡(P∧Q)∨(P∧R); P∨(Q∧R)|≡(P∨Q)∧(P∨R)]
- The Absorption Laws:
[MATH: P∧(P∨Q)|≡P; P∨(P∧Q)|≡P]

Item 14 — Example: Using Laws Involving Conjunction and Disjunction

Example Prompt:
Write a sentence that is equivalent to the following: "[MATH: x] is an integer, and [MATH: x] is negative and it is an integer."

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Using the commutative law, we can replace the phrase "[MATH: x] is negative and it is an integer" with the phrase "[MATH: x] is an integer and it is negative." The sentence now reads

> "[MATH: x] is an integer, and [MATH: x] is an integer and it is negative."

Then, using the associative law, we can move the comma:

> "[MATH: x] is an integer and [MATH: x] is an integer, and it is negative."

Now, we can simplify the phrase "[MATH: x] is an integer and [MATH: x] is an integer" to just "[MATH: x] is an integer" The sentence now reads

> "[MATH: x] is an integer, and it is negative."

Finally, we can write the sentence more concisely:

> "[MATH: x] is a negative integer."
